<!-- Section 2: Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Numerical Formulations</div>
<h2>7.1 The Classical Runge-Kutta Method (RK4)</h2>
<p>Approximating initial value problem $y' = f(t, y)$ with step size $h = \Delta t$:</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="eq-box">
$$y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{6}(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)$$
</div>

<p>Where the four intermediate stage slopes are evaluated sequentially:</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n) \\
k_2 &= f(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2}, y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_1) \\
k_3 &= f(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2}, y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_2) \\
k_4 &= f(t_n + h, y_n + h k_3)
\end{aligned}$$
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 3: Stability -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-stability">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">02 · Numerical Stability</div>
<h2>7.2 Dahlquist Test Equation & Absolute Stability</h2>
<p>Applying numerical integrators to linear scalar test problem $y' = \lambda y$ where $z = \lambda h \in \mathbb{C}$:</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="callout">
<strong>• Forward Euler ($y_{n+1} = (1 + z) y_n$):</strong> Stable only inside the unit disc $|1 + z| \le 1$. Requires tiny step size $h < 2/|\lambda_{\max}|$.<br>
<strong>• Classical RK4 ($y_{n+1} = (1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24}) y_n$):</strong> Enlarged stability region on negative real axis spanning $-2.78 \le \operatorname{Re}(z) \le 0$.<br>
<strong>• Backward Euler ($y_{n+1} = (1 - z)^{-1} y_n$):</strong> $A$-stable! Stable across the entire left complex half-plane $\operatorname{Re}(z) \le 0$, allowing unconditional stability regardless of system stiffness.
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 4: Misconceptions -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Is a Stiff System Just a Fast-Oscillating System?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
No. Stiffness is not merely about rapid dynamics; it is about <strong>disparity of timescales</strong> where fast transient modes decay quickly, leaving slow dynamics of physical interest.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
In stiff mechanics, explicit integrators are forced to take microscopic time steps (e.g. $\Delta t < 10^{-6}\text{ s}$) solely to keep the already-decayed fast mode from exploding numerically, even when the actual solution is changing smoothly! Switching to an $A$-stable implicit solver (such as Radau or BDF) removes this stability barrier entirely.
</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-quiz">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">03 · Diagnostic Checkpoint</div>
<h2>7.3 Check Your Understanding</h2>
<p>Test your understanding of numerical stiffness and step size constraints.</p>
</div>

<div class="quiz-box">
<div class="quiz-question">
<strong>Question:</strong> A mechanical ODE has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = -1\text{ s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda_2 = -5000\text{ s}^{-1}$. If using Forward Euler, what is the maximum time step $h$ before the numerical simulation explodes?
</div>
<div class="quiz-options">
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="h = 2.0 s would explode immediately! Stability is governed strictly by the fastest (most negative) eigenvalue lambda2!">
A. $h < 2.0\text{ s}$ based on $\lambda_1$.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="true" data-explanation="Forward Euler stability boundary requires |1 + lambda * h| <= 1, which for real negative lambda means -2 <= lambda * h <= 0, or h < 2 / |lambda_max| = 2 / 5000 = 0.0004 seconds! Even though lambda2 decays in 1 millisecond, explicit Euler must take tiny steps forever.">
B. $h < 0.0004\text{ s}$ ($0.4\text{ milliseconds}$) dictated by the stiff eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = -5000\text{ s}^{-1}$.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Euler is conditionally stable, not unconditionally stable.">
C. Any time step is permitted as long as energy is conserved.
</div>
</div>

<!-- Section 6: Code -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>7.4 Stiff ODE Integration Benchmark</h2>
<p>Compare explicit RK45 against implicit Radau on a stiff mechanical system.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (SciPy RK45 vs Radau)</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

# Stiff spring-damper system: lambda1 = -1, lambda2 = -2000
def stiff_odes(t, y):
    return [-y[0], -2000.0 * (y[1] - np.sin(t))]

t_span = [0, 5.0]
y0 = [1.0, 0.0]

# Explicit RK45 (encounters step-size bottleneck)
sol_rk45 = solve_ivp(stiff_odes, t_span, y0, method='RK45')
print(f"Explicit RK45 step count: {sol_rk45.nfev} function evaluations")

# Implicit Radau (A-stable, takes large smooth steps)
sol_radau = solve_ivp(stiff_odes, t_span, y0, method='Radau')
print(f"Implicit Radau step count: {sol_radau.nfev} evaluations (Orders of magnitude faster!)")</code></pre>
</div>
</section>
